title: Prompt Sets, Benchmarks, and Regression Triage: Applied ML Guide
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:

This document defines Redwood Inference’s standards and playbooks for prompt sets and benchmarks, how those artifacts integrate with the eval harness, model onboarding and quantization profile inclusion, and the regression triage process used to investigate quality degradations. It collects prescriptive guidance, templates, and step-by-step procedures so product, applied ML, and SRE teams can operate a stable, auditable evaluation pipeline.

Scope:

- Applicable to models and model variants being considered for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Covers the lifecycle of prompt sets and benchmarks from creation -> review -> scheduled runs -> drift monitoring -> regression triage.
- Includes integration notes for quantization profiles and how to validate post-quantization quality.

Goals:

- Provide reproducible, reviewable prompt sets and benchmark jobs that map to customer-facing behaviors.
- Detect and triage regressions within 48 hours of detection.
- Ensure quantized model variants meet minimum quality thresholds before rollout.

Key Definitions:

- Prompt set: A curated collection of prompts designed to evaluate a specific capability or behavior (e.g., summarization fidelity, api-integration completions, safety red-team checks).
- Benchmark: A named collection of prompt sets plus metrics and evaluation scripts used for tracking model quality over time.
- Eval harness: The standardized CI/automation system that runs benchmarks, collects metrics, stores artifacts, and produces changelogs.
- Regression: A statistically significant degradation in one or more benchmarked metrics relative to the pinned baseline for a model version.

Roles and Ownership:

- Applied ML (primary): owns prompt set design, metric definitions, and baseline selection.
- Product (secondary): defines product-facing behaviors and acceptance criteria for new prompts/benchmarks.
- Eng SRE / Serving Runtime: provides throughput/latency constraints and ensures evaluation runs are representative of production sequences.
- QA / Solutions Engineering: performs acceptance tests for especially customer-visible flows.

Prompt Set Lifecycle (recommended process):

1. Proposal: create a prompt-set proposal page describing intent, coverage, example prompts, and metrics. Include a named owner and approximate expected sensitivity.
2. Review: at least two reviewers from Applied ML and Product must sign off. Document corner cases and failure modes.
3. Staging run: add prompt set to the eval harness under a '‘staging’' benchmark for 2 full runs across typical sequence-length distributions (short, medium, long).
4. Promote: upon passing staging thresholds, add the prompt set to the canonical benchmark and schedule it for daily/weekly runs as appropriate.

Design guidance for prompt sets:

- Keep each prompt set focused (1 capability). Typical sizes: 200-2,000 prompts depending on variability.
- Use stratified sampling across user intents, domain vocabulary, and sequence length.
- Include explicit negative examples / adversarial cases for safety-related sets.
- Provide a human-annotated gold label when metric requires exact match or graded scoring.

Benchmarking standards and metric definitions:

- Use deterministic seeding for sampling runs and record seeds as part of artifacts.
- Minimum metrics per benchmark:
  - Accuracy / Exact Match (when applicable)
  - ROUGE/Lexical F1 or BERTScore for open-ended text tasks
  - Safety score (binary/graded) for guardrail prompt sets
  - Latency P50/P95 and tokens-per-second for performance-sensitive benchmarks
  - Cost-per-request estimate using current serving config

- Acceptance thresholds: Benchmarks must include a target baseline value and an alert threshold. Example: Summary-Fidelity benchmark baseline = BERTScore 0.81; alert if new run < 0.78.

Example benchmark table (text format):

| Benchmark name | Primary metric | Baseline | Alert threshold | Run cadence | Owner |
| Summary-Fidelity | BERTScore | 0.81 | 0.78 | daily | applied-ml |
| Code-Completion-Safety | SafetyScore | 0.995 | 0.990 | hourly | applied-ml |

Integration with Eval Harness (practical steps):

- Files: place prompt sets under prompt_catalog/{benchmark_name}/{prompt_set_name}.jsonl with schema documented in the prompt catalog README.
- CI job: create or update a Jenkins/GitHub Actions workflow that runs the harness container with the specific model tag and collects artifacts to S3. Use the standardized run.sh wrapper: 

  ./run_benchmark.sh --benchmark Summary-Fidelity --model-tag v2.3.1 --seed 42 --output s3://redwood-evals/summary-fidelity/v2.3.1/2026-07-15

- Artifacts produced: predictions.jsonl, metrics.json, seeds.txt, run_config.yaml, logs.tar.gz. Post-run the harness will create a changelog entry with diff against baseline.

Model Onboarding Checklist (eval-related):

1. Model card authored with architecture, training data provenance, and recommended serving configs.
2. Baseline benchmark run on canonical benchmark suite at 3 sequence-length buckets.
3. Quantization profile evaluation (see below) executed and compared to fp16 baseline.
4. Safety and guardrail prompt sets executed with manual review of any failures.
5. Sign off by Applied ML and Product; update model onboarding record in the eval-harness registry.

Quantization Profile Integration and Validation:

- Purpose: include quantization variants in the eval harness to identify accuracy regressions introduced by lower-precision kernels.
- Profiles: profiles are named artifacts that include per-layer quantization parameters and expected perf estimates (e.g., q8_0-layerwise, q4f_fast).
- Validation steps:
  1. Run canonical benchmark on fp16 or reference full-precision model.
  2. Run same benchmark on quantized variant using identical seeds and sampling.
  3. Compute metric deltas and flag any metric with delta > configured tolerance (per-benchmark tolerance table).
  4. If any guardrail or safety prompt fails, block promotion and create a regression ticket.

- Acceptance rule (example): for NLU/QA tasks, allow up to 0.5% absolute drop in exact-match; for summarization allow up to 1.5% BERTScore drop. Performance improvements (latency or cost) must be documented to justify acceptance.

Regression Triage Playbook (high-level procedure):

1. Detection: alert triggered by automated monitoring on metrics.json or by a human report. Include run-id and diff to baseline in the alert.
2. Initial validation (within 4 hours): rerun the failing benchmark with identical run_config and a fresh seed set to rule out transient failures. Attach new artifacts to the incident ticket.
3. Scope analysis (within 12 hours): determine if regression is model-specific, quantization-specific, or infra-related by running:
   - baseline model at same commit
   - affected model on a different host/hardware class
   - quantized vs fp16 variants
4. Root cause hypotheses: consider model drift (new training data), tokenization changes, prompting changes, scoring/eval harness bug, or runtime kernel mismatch.
5. Block or mitigate: if regression impacts safety or customer SLAs, rollback the serving model or route traffic to fallback variant. If degradation is limited to non-critical metrics, schedule a hotfix/roll-forward.
6. Remediation and verification: implement fix, run full canonical benchmark and a targeted smoke test, and close the ticket when metrics return to within acceptance thresholds.
7. Postmortem: for regressions requiring rollback or customer impact, produce a 72-hour postmortem documenting cause, mitigation, timeline, and long-term actions.

Triage checklist (quick):

- [ ] reproduce run locally with identical seed
- [ ] compare tokenization outputs for a sample of failing prompts
- [ ] run with and without quantization profile
- [ ] verify eval harness scoring code version matches baseline
- [ ] collect runtime logs and GPU/CPU telemetry

Communication and runbook links:

- Primary incident channel: #applied-ml-regressions
- Pager policy: applied-ml-oncall (EScalate if regression is safety critical or affects >5% of production traffic)
- Runbooks: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/applied-ml-eval-harness-standards-2025

Appendix: Example prompt set JSONL schema (single-line JSON per prompt):

{
  "id": "prompt-0001",
  "prompt": "Summarize the following article in two sentences:",
  "metadata": {"domain": "news", "length_bucket": "short"},
  "gold": "<human reference summary>"
}

Notes and best practices:

- Maintain transparency: add a short description and owner field to each prompt file explaining selection criteria.
- Version everything: prompt sets, benchmarks, and quantization profiles must be versioned and immutable once promoted. Use tags like v1.0.0 in the harness registry.
- Auditability: keep human labels and small adjudication notes for ambiguous examples; store them with the artifact bundle for future review.
- Reuse: prefer referencing canonical prompt sets rather than duplicating similar prompts across benchmarks.

If you are adding a new prompt set or benchmark, follow the Prompt Set Lifecycle steps above and contact the Applied ML team for a pairing review. For urgent regressions, follow the Regression Triage Playbook and escalate on #applied-ml-regressions if you need assistance with a rollback or fallback routing.
